clinicalPearls: Seminoma is the commonest single germ cell tumour type and tends to present slightly later than non-seminomatous tumours, usually as a painless testicular mass
By definition AFP is normal in pure seminoma; a raised AFP means a non-seminomatous element is present and the tumour is managed as NSGCT even if histology looks purely seminomatous
Beta-hCG may be modestly elevated (from syncytiotrophoblastic cells) and LDH reflects tumour bulk, but neither excludes the diagnosis of seminoma
Radical inguinal orchidectomy establishes the diagnosis and provides local control; trans-scrotal approaches are avoided
Seminoma is highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive, so stage I disease may be managed by surveillance, adjuvant carboplatin, or adjuvant radiotherapy after individualised discussion
Cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy is the mainstay for higher-stage or metastatic disease, with radiotherapy or chemotherapy chosen by stage and risk
Sperm banking should be offered before treatment given the risks to fertility
reference.pathophysiology: Seminoma arises from germ cell neoplasia in situ and is composed of relatively uniform cells that resemble undifferentiated primordial germ cells, often with a lymphocytic infiltrate and granulomatous reaction within the tumour. A minority contain syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells that secrete beta-hCG, accounting for mild marker elevation, but seminoma cells do not produce AFP. Like other germ cell tumours it carries isochromosome 12p and spreads predominantly by lymphatics to the retroperitoneal nodes before later haematogenous dissemination.
additionalDifferentials: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumour or mixed germ cell tumour
Spermatocytic tumour (a distinct, generally indolent entity)
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound demonstrating a solid intratesticular lesion
Serum AFP (expected normal), beta-hCG, and LDH before and after orchidectomy
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for staging
Semen analysis and sperm banking before treatment
Repeat marker measurement to confirm normalisation after treatment
redFlags: Bulky retroperitoneal nodal disease or visceral metastases
A raised AFP indicating an occult non-seminomatous component requiring NSGCT management
Markers failing to normalise after orchidectomy
Rapidly enlarging mass with systemic symptoms
reference.prognosis: Pure seminoma has an excellent prognosis, with cure rates approaching those of other stages of testicular cancer; localised disease is almost universally curable and even metastatic seminoma has high cure rates with cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
pitfalls: Assuming any germ cell tumour with a raised AFP can be treated as seminoma
Interpreting a mildly raised beta-hCG as excluding seminoma
Using a trans-scrotal biopsy and risking seeding
Omitting sperm banking before radiotherapy or chemotherapy
Failing to monitor for a metachronous contralateral tumour on follow-up
